correctness.rationale: Two-sided Cauchy estimates on |z|=e^{±b} give decay e^{−b|n|} for every b<a. Exact internal factorization makes any member an m-fold product for each m, so multiplication of coefficients improves b to mb, giving a unique continuation in particular to Ω_{2a}. The graph of that linear extension is closed by continuous restriction and the identity theorem; closedness of V gives the needed Fréchet domain. For any a<b₁<2a its larger-annulus seminorm is controlled by a single smaller compact-annulus norm p_{b₀}, which then generates the topology of V. The p_{b₀}-unit ball is uniformly bounded on the larger compact annulus and Montel supplies relative compactness in p_{b₀}; completeness makes the ball compact. Thus V is finite-dimensional. An injective finite coordinate restriction exists by separation of points; using distinct nonzero generic evaluation values, zero-constant interpolation constructs orthogonal idempotents, with identities holding on all coordinates by injectivity. Their 0–1 coefficients tend to zero at both ends, so the supports are finite, and orthogonality gives disjointness. The idempotents span, are exactly the primitive ones, and finite block elements have internal coefficientwise square roots. The zero space and closedness of the converse are accounted for. This is a proof check, with no finite certificate needed.

evidence: Ben-Simon gives ambient powers and the maximal dense nonclosed family; the bounded-family theorem excludes all nonzero linear subspaces. The ideal statements have an additional ideal hypothesis and allow infinite-dimensional closed ideals without claiming internal factorization.
broader_coverage.reasoning: Neither the bounded-family case nor a classification of closed or finite-dimensional ideals covers arbitrary closed self-reproducing linear spaces. In particular, a block containing two indices gives a non-ideal that cannot come from the ideal results. The broader 1996 article remains an access risk, not a demonstrated exclusion.

evidence: Ben-Simon's Theorem 5.2 identifies ambient m-fold products with restrictions from a wider annulus; Theorem 5.3 therefore controls where an arbitrary self-reproducing family lies, not its closed subspaces. The ideal classification is not a general subalgebra theorem.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: The continuation theorem can replace the first step of the submitted proof and is not itself new. Containment in a dense continuation class supplies neither finite dimension of a closed subspace nor its idempotents: one must use closedness to turn memberwise continuation into a uniform seminorm bound and then exploit compactness, followed by the separate non-ideal block argument. No inspected prior statement supplies that classification.

evidence: The Laurent coefficient transform is an algebra isomorphism onto the Köthe-type space with finite weighted ℓ¹ seminorms ∑ₙ |xₙ|e^{b|n|} for every 0<b<a. Pirkovskii studies the product span of a Köthe algebra and its relationship to squares.
equivalent_formulations.reasoning: The sequence formulation is genuinely equivalent for this ambient space, but a general identity about squares and the product span of a Köthe algebra does not classify the arbitrary closed linear subspaces of that particular space with internal exact factorization. The topology and closedness condition are decisive.

value.rationale: The theorem separates a familiar dense infinite-dimensional self-reproducing family from closed ones, for which exact factorization forces finite dimension. It identifies every surviving family, not only its dimension or the ideal cases. The exact role of compact-open closedness and the description of non-ideal blocks make a useful structural classification.
